id: Daily Trials by a Sensitive Man

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Oh, there are times When all this fret and tumult that we hear Do seem more stale than to the sexton’s ear His own dull chimes. Ding dong! ding dong! The world is in a simmer like a sea Over a pent volcano,—woe is me All the day long! From crib to shroud! Nurse o’er our cradles screameth lullaby, And friends in boots tramp round us as we die, Snuffling aloud. At morning’s call The small-voiced pug-dog welcomes in the sun, And flea-bit mongrels, wakening one by one, Give answer all. When evening dim Draws round us, then the lonely caterwaul, Tart solo, sour duet, and general squall,— These are our hymn. Women, with tongues Like polar needles, ever on the jar; Men, plugless word-spouts, whose deep fountains are Within their lungs. Children, with drums Strapped round them by the fond paternal ass; Peripatetics with a blade of grass Between their thumbs. Vagrants, whose arts Have caged some devil in their mad machine, Which grinding, squeaks, with husky groans between, Come out by starts. Cockneys that kill Thin horses of a Sunday,—men, with clams, Hoarse as young bisons roaring for their dams From hill to hill. Soldiers, with guns, Making a nuisance of the blessed air, Child-crying bellman, children in despair, Screeching for buns. Storms, thunders, waves! Howl, crash, and bellow till ye get your fill; Ye sometimes rest; men never can be still But in their graves.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem attacks the relentless noise of human life, using comic exaggeration and a catalog of everyday disturbances from infancy to death. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, His, Ding

outputs.L1:
Oh, there are times when all this fret and tumult that we hear  
Do seem more stale than to the sexton’s ear  
His own dull chimes.  

Ding dong! ding dong!  

The world is in a simmer like a sea  
Over a pent volcano,—woe is me  
All the day long!  

From crib to shroud!  

Nurse o’er our cradles screameth lullaby,  
And friends in boots tramp round us as we die,  
Snuffling aloud.  

At morning’s call,  
The small-voiced pug-dog welcomes in the sun,  
And flea-bit mongrels, wakening one by one,  
Give answer all.  

When evening dim  
Draws round us, then the lonely caterwaul,  
Tart solo, sour duet, and general squall,—  
These are our hymn.  

Women, with tongues  
Like polar needles, ever on the jar;  
Men, plugless word-spouts, whose deep fountains are  
Within their lungs.  

Children, with drums  
Strapped round them by the fond paternal ass;  
Peripatetics with a blade of grass  
Between their thumbs.  

Vagrants, whose arts  
Have caged some devil in their mad machine,  
Which, grinding, squeaks, with husky groans between,  
Come out by starts.  

Cockneys that kill  
Thin horses of a Sunday,—men, with clams,  
Hoarse as young bisons roaring for their dams  
From hill to hill.  

Soldiers, with guns,  
Making a nuisance of the blessed air;  
Child-crying bellman, children in despair,  
Screeching for buns.  

Storms, thunders, waves!  
Howl, crash, and bellow till ye get your fill;  
Ye sometimes rest; men never can be still  
But in their graves.
outputs.L2:
Ah, there are moments when the strain and uproar surrounding us seem even more wearisome than a gravedigger finds the flat ringing of his own bells. Ding-dong, ding-dong! The whole earth seethes like an ocean boiling above a hidden volcano—alas, all through the day!

From the cradle to the coffin, noise attends us. A nurse shrieks a lullaby over our infancy, and when we are dying, booted friends stamp around us, loudly sniffling.

At daybreak, the tiny-voiced pug greets the rising sun, and the flea-ridden curs, waking one after another, all reply.

When dusky evening closes in, the solitary yowling of cats begins: sharp solos, bitter duets, and one great collective shriek. These become our evening song.

Women’s tongues swing and quiver like compass needles near the pole, always unsettled. Men are endless spouts of speech without stoppers, their deep reservoirs of sound lodged in their lungs.

Children march about with drums fastened to them by some loving but foolish father. Wandering walkers whistle through blades of grass pressed between their thumbs.

Tramps possess strange devices, as if some demon had been trapped inside their frantic machines, which grind and squeal, letting out rough groans in jerks and bursts.

City folk spend Sundays killing worn-out horses; men selling clams shout themselves hoarse, bellowing like young buffalo calling for their mothers across the hills.

Soldiers fire their guns, fouling the blessed air with racket. Bellmen cry out like children, and children themselves wail in misery, shrieking for buns.

Storms, thunder, and waves may howl, smash, and roar until they have had enough; at least they sometimes fall silent. Human beings, however, are never quiet except in their graves.
outputs.L3:
The speaker laments that the constant noise and agitation of the world has grown stale, tiresome, and almost unbearable. What might once have seemed lively or amusing now feels exhausting, as if the whole world is trapped in a cycle of disturbance and unrest. Everywhere the speaker turns, there is some new sound, some fresh interruption, and no place appears to offer peace.

Human life is presented as being surrounded by noise from its very beginning to its end. At birth, a child enters the world amid cries, bustle, and the clamor of nurses. From that first moment, life is marked by sound and commotion. This continues throughout a person’s days, until even death fails to bring immediate quiet, since mourners gather with their own cries, lamentations, and rituals of grief. In this way, the poem suggests that human existence is enclosed by noise on all sides.

The natural world, too, contributes to this endless clamor. Animals such as dogs and cats fill the day with barking, howling, and mewing, adding their voices to the general confusion. From morning until evening, their sounds mingle with the noises of human activity, creating an atmosphere in which silence seems impossible. Even ordinary life becomes a kind of continual disturbance.

People of every sort also add to the din. Their chatter, songs, street cries, arguments, music, and daily occupations all create a restless soundscape. The streets are filled with calls and interruptions; weapons, tools, and household noises further intensify the disorder. No class or profession is exempt: everyone contributes in some way to the overwhelming noise of the world.

The poem contrasts the unavoidable sounds of nature with the particular restlessness of human beings. While animal noises may be part of the ordinary rhythm of life, human noise appears excessive, anxious, and self-perpetuating. The speaker’s weariness comes not simply from sound itself, but from the sense that humanity cannot be still. Ultimately, the poem suggests that true silence can only be found in death, when the agitation of life finally comes to an end.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a comic but bitter attack on the endless noise produced by human life. Rather than treating noise as a minor inconvenience, the speaker exaggerates it into a defining feature of existence itself. From the moment a baby cries at birth to the final sounds surrounding death and burial, human beings are shown as creatures who never stop making or causing disturbance. The poem builds its satire through a crowded catalog of everyday noises: crying children, quarrelling adults, street sounds, domestic commotion, work, travel, ceremony, and social chatter. This accumulation creates the impression that life in human society is one long, inescapable uproar.

The humor of the poem comes from its exaggeration and its rapid piling up of examples. Ordinary sounds are made to seem absurdly oppressive, as if every stage of life contributes to a universal conspiracy against peace and quiet. Yet beneath the comedy is a darker view of society. The poem suggests that human restlessness is not accidental but permanent. People are noisy because they are always demanding, competing, complaining, celebrating, grieving, or interfering with one another. Human life appears as a cycle of agitation, with no true silence available while one remains part of the social world.

The poem contrasts this human clamor with the noise of nature. Thunder, storms, wind, and other natural uproars may be loud, but they are temporary. However violent they become, they eventually pass, leaving calm behind. Human noise, by contrast, is continuous. It follows the individual from infancy through adulthood and ends only in the grave. This comparison makes nature seem almost merciful when set against society: natural disturbances may be frightening, but at least they stop.

By ending with the idea that only death brings release from human noise, the poem turns its comic complaint into bleak satire. It mocks not just loud sounds, but the whole restless condition of human existence. The speaker’s preference for natural uproar over human clamor reveals a deep weariness with society and its constant activity. In this way, the poem uses humor, exaggeration, and everyday detail to express a grim conclusion: the world of people is so noisy and unsettled that peace can be found only outside society—or after life itself has ended.
outputs.L5:
When the old clock began to **ding**, everyone in the room turned to look. It was a sound they had heard many times before, but this time it felt different. **His** face grew thoughtful as he listened, as if the ringing had reminded him of something important.

**When** the final note faded, he stood up and smiled. “Sometimes,” he said, “a simple sound can bring back a memory, a lesson, or a moment we thought we had forgotten.”

The quiet returned, but the meaning of that small **ding** stayed with them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-style satirical poem about the unbearable noises of city life, with rhymed quatrains and archaic diction.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Ballad of the Bawling Metropolis**

O hark! the morn with brazen throat  
Doth split the fog’s begrimed repose,  
While carts, like demons half-afloat,  
Go thundering o’er the pauper’s toes.  

The costermonger, crowned with grime,  
Proclaims his pears with lungs of brass;  
He shrieks “Fine fruit!” five hundredth time,  
And shames the donkey as they pass.  

The omnibus, that wooden whale,  
Doth groan and creak and cough and roar;  
Its driver, flourishing his flail,  
Cries “Room!” and murders peace once more.  

The chimney-sweep with sable grin  
Pipes forth a note both sharp and thin;  
If angels heard that impish din,  
They’d bolt the gates and lock him in.  

The organ-man beneath my pane  
Grinds “Home, Sweet Home” till home be hell;  
His monkey capers in my brain,  
And rings my nerves like Bow Church bell.  

The peddler bawls of pins and lace,  
The fishwife hymns her haddock’s fame;  
Each blessed tradesman in the place  
Regards my headache as his game.  

The newsboy, imp of ink and steam,  
Doth cry disasters down the street;  
His “Murder!” wakes me from a dream  
Where silence kissed my slippered feet.  

Then clatter, bang, and shriek, and bray,  
Compose the city’s noble psalm;  
By night one prays to steal away—  
By dawn one prays to keep one’s calm.  

O London! grand, infernal hive,  
Where Progress beats her iron drum,  
How strange that any soul survive,  
Nor instantly grow deaf and dumb.  

Give me, kind Fate, some mossy cell  
Where only owls and beetles speak;  
For they, compared with urban yell,  
Are drawing-room divines and meek.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a humorous 19th-century poem complaining about constant human and animal noise, from barking dogs to street musicians and soldiers.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Complaint Against the Noises of Creation**

O Muse! if thou hast cotton-wool,  
Pray stuff it in mine ear;  
For all the world, by knave and fool,  
Is making noises here.

The dog beneath my chamber-pane  
Barks treason at the moon;  
The cat replies in shrieks of pain,  
Though marriage comes in June.

The milkman clatters pails at four,  
The sweep begins at five;  
By six the newsboys at my door  
Proclaim the realm alive.

A barrel-organ, gaunt and grim,  
Comes grinding up the street,  
And murders, in a minor hymn,  
All airs once counted sweet.

The fiddler scrapes, the cornet blows,  
The drummer thumps his hide;  
A German band, in martial throes,  
Assaults the other side.

Then tramp the soldiers, red and stout,  
With fifes of piercing tone,  
As if the foe they meant to rout  
Were lodged within my bone.

The cabman cracks his whip like doom,  
The costermonger cries;  
The baby in the upper room  
Competes for morning prize.

The donkey brays, the parrot swears,  
The rooster calls the sun;  
And every creature, unawares,  
Declares itself the one.

O London! mighty, muddy mart,  
Where bells and bedlams meet,  
Thou hast a loud, industrious heart—  
And very noisy feet.

If Heaven grants me any grace,  
When life’s last inn I keep,  
Pray set me in some silent place—  
Where even ghosts must sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem in the style of Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. about urban clamor and the impossibility of silence.
counterfactuals.output:
**The City’s Never-Silent Bell**

I sought a nook where Silence dwelt,  
A shy, sequestered thing,  
Where not a wheel on granite smote,  
Nor wires were taught to sing;  
I found a room above the street,  
With curtains drawn with care—  
And heard the city’s iron feet  
Go trampling up the stair.

The drays went groaning by below,  
The newsboys piped their cries,  
The hammers beat a brazen tune  
That clattered to the skies;  
The steeple shook its solemn tongue,  
The engine shrieked in glee,  
And every pane, like captive glass,  
Kept humming company.

“Be still!” I cried; the pavement laughed,  
The crossing answered “Nay!”  
The horse’s hoof, the vendor’s horn,  
The bells across the way,  
The far-off forge, the nearer cart,  
The latch, the clock, the door—  
All took my little prayer apart  
And flung it on the floor.

For Silence, in the city’s breast,  
Is but a courteous name;  
She wears a veil of soot and mist  
And never comes the same.  
She hides between two thunderclaps,  
She lingers in a breath,  
Then starts to hear the milkman’s cans  
Go jangling under death.

O happy fields, where once I dreamed  
The winds alone might pass!  
Yet even there the cricket saws  
His fiddle in the grass;  
The brook repeats its silver tale,  
The robin wakes the tree—  
The world was fashioned with a voice,  
And will not voiceless be.

Then let the anvils ring their psalm,  
The chimneys drone their bass;  
Let commerce, with a thousand throats,  
Roar in the market-place.  
Who asks for perfect stillness asks  
What earth can never give—  
The hush before creation spoke,  
Not granted while we live.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a rhyming poem that begins “Oh, there are times” and laments the fret, tumult, bells, dogs, children, and street sounds of the world.
counterfactuals.output:
Oh, there are times when weary hearts would flee  
The fret and tumult of the world away,  
Where bells ring out across the troubled lea,  
And clanging hours consume the quiet day.  

The dogs cry sharp beneath the window-pane,  
The children shout along the stony street,  
The wheels go grinding through the dust and rain,  
And restless footsteps hurry, beat by beat.  

The vendors call, the iron hinges scream,  
The shutters bang, the crowded crossings roar;  
Peace fades like starlight in a fevered dream,  
And silence slips her hand from every door.  

Oh, for some vale where softened shadows fall,  
Where winds speak low and silver waters gleam—  
Far from the bells, the cries, the dogs, the call,  
To rest at last inside a soundless dream.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a mock-serious poetic rant about noise pollution, ending with the idea that only the grave is quiet.
counterfactuals.output:
O clatter, thou tin-crowned tyrant of the breakfast hour—  
must every spoon declare war upon the bowl?  
Must every bus exhale like a wounded dragon  
beneath my window, at precisely dawn,  
when even the sun has the decency to rise in silence?

Behold the modern city:  
a cathedral built for jackhammers,  
where sirens practice opera,  
where leaf blowers preach their gasoline sermons,  
where phones chirp, blink, bleat, and demand devotion  
like tiny gods with cracked plastic faces.

No bird may sing without accompaniment.  
No thought may stretch its legs.  
Even the refrigerator mutters at midnight,  
a cold little philosopher with a motorized soul.

And we, poor citizens of the Great Racket,  
smile politely while motorcycles split the air in half,  
while upstairs furniture migrates in thunderous herds,  
while someone, somewhere, discovers a subwoofer  
and mistakes vibration for personality.

I ask not for luxury.  
I ask not for palaces, pearls, or obedient weather.  
I ask for one soft minute  
unpunctured by honk, hum, howl, drill, buzz, bark, beep—  
one moment in which the mind may sit down  
without wearing a helmet.

But no. The world bangs its pots.  
The age coughs into amplifiers.  
Progress arrives with backup alarms.

So let the scholars debate,  
let the committees convene beneath fluorescent buzzing,  
let the neighbors test their speakers against the wrath of heaven.  
I have seen the truth carved plainly in stone:

Peace is not zoned, licensed, funded, or found.  
Silence keeps its last apartment underground.  
Only the grave is quiet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
